name: Chin tucks

lead: A chin tuck draws the head straight back over the neck so the chin moves in without tilting down. People do it to fix a head carried forward of the shoulders and, in some accounts, to sharpen the jaw and neck line.

Proponents say it strengthens the deep neck flexors and counters forward head posture, which they link to a more defined jaw-neck profile. Published studies are mostly in swallowing (dysphagia) research, where the posture changes pharyngeal dimensions and pressure; studies of facial appearance were not found.

paras: People do chin tucks as holds or repetitions during the day or in posture routines, often paired with rows and face pulls for forward head posture. A resisted version, chin tuck against resistance, has also been studied for neck muscle activity.

No serious harms are documented in the sources reviewed. One forum thread author claims long holds could strain the cervical spine, which other users in the thread disputed; no study cited here tests it. People with neck pain or injury may prefer clinician advice.

angle.text: Users do chin tucks to improve head posture and, in some accounts, to sharpen the jaw and neck line by pulling the head back over the shoulders. Research mostly concerns swallowing therapy and neck muscle activity.

lead: A chin tuck is a posture or exercise in which the head is retracted backward over the neck so that the chin draws in. In clinical literature the term most often refers to a swallowing maneuver used with people who have dysphagia, and it has been studied with videofluoroscopy and manometry [1][2][3][4]. A resisted version, chin tuck against resistance (CTAR), was proposed as a way to increase activity of the suprahyoid muscles [5].

In looksmaxxing communities the movement is discussed in connection with posture and head position, in the belief that a head held forward weakens the appearance of the jawline and neck. Forward head posture is described by Wikipedia as a common postural pattern linked to prolonged device use, with deep neck flexor strengthening among the proposed remedies [6]. No clinical study located here has measured whether chin tucks change facial or jaw appearance.
infobox: Deep neck flexors (proposed); suprahyoid muscles in the resisted variant
None (resisted variants use a ball or band)

paras: The movement involves retracting the head horizontally while keeping the gaze level, rather than nodding the head downward. A looksmax.org user attributes a version called the McKenzie chin tuck to the orthotropics advocate Mike Mew and says it rotates the head into flexion.

Most studies examine chin tuck as a swallowing posture. A manometry study of seven subjects compared neutral, head-turn and chin-tuck conditions for pharyngeal pressure events [1]. Videomanometry studies tested supraglottic swallow, effortful swallow and chin tuck in eight healthy volunteers and in eight patients with pharyngeal dysfunction [2][3]. A 2002 report from the same line of work examined hypopharyngeal intrabolus pressure [7]. A radiographic study of 30 subjects measured pharyngeal dimensions in neutral and chin-tucked positions [8], and a clinical and electrophysiologic study examined how head and neck positions affect oropharyngeal swallowing [4].

The resisted variant, CTAR, was described in a 2014 paper as a Shaker-type exercise designed to raise suprahyoid muscle activity [5]. Reviews of dysphagia management after stroke and swallowing rehabilitation after oropharyngeal cancer surgery mention chin-tuck-based approaches in rehabilitation contexts [9][10]. These studies concern swallowing, not posture or facial appearance.

Wikipedia describes forward head posture as common among device users and some occupations, with proposed effects including neck muscle fatigue and cervicogenic headache and proposed remedies including deep neck flexor strengthening, mid-back strengthening, thoracic mobilization and ergonomic changes. The article carries maintenance notes about weak sourcing for some treatment claims [6].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the chin tuck appears in threads about neck posture and jaw appearance, where users ask what it does and debate its safety.

claims.claim: Chin tucks improve head posture by stretching the neck.
Prolonged chin-tuck holds can damage the neck.
Sleeping or holding a different head position could improve the jaw.
